source.heading: Where Collins said it

docMeta.dd: Alan M. Webber, Fast Company founding editor
2001, tied to Collins’s October 2001 Fast Company cover story

source.excerpt: I believe it’s more a matter of cause and effect than an accident. There is something directly related between the absence of celebrity and the presence of good-to-great results. Why? First, when you have a celebrity, the company turns into “the one genius with 1,000 helpers.” It creates a sense that the whole thing is really about the CEO.
trail: 2001: In a Web-exclusive Fast Company interview with Alan M. Webber, Collins says “There is something directly related between the absence of celebrity and the presence of good-to-great results” (archived article ↗).
2013 capture: The earliest Wayback copy of the page has the same “something directly related” wording (2013 snapshot ↗).

Wikiquote: Quotes the passage as “There is a direct relationship between the absence of celebrity and the presence of good-to-great results,” citing Fast Company online magazine, October 2001 (Wikiquote ↗).
Quote sites: Aggregators repeat the “direct relationship” version without naming a source (example ↗).
source.excerptNote: Collins is answering a question about why the CEOs of the good-to-great companies were “largely anonymous.” Wikiquote’s version of this passage starts “There is a direct relationship…” and leaves out a sentence that follows in the published text (“And that leads to all sorts of problems…”).

author.name: Jim Collins
author.heading: About Jim Collins
author.bio: James C. “Jim” Collins is an American researcher, author and speaker on how companies grow and last. He taught on the faculty of the Stanford Graduate School of Business and co-wrote Built to Last (1994) with Jerry I. Porras. His Good to Great (2001) introduced the idea of Level 5 leadership: humble, low-profile leaders who put the company ahead of their own fame.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Jim Collins, from his 2001 Fast Company interview “Good Questions, Great Answers.” The exact published words are “something directly related,” not “a direct relationship” (archived article ↗).

context.heading: Why Collins said it
lead: The interview came out alongside Good to Great (2001), Collins’s study of companies that moved from average results to lasting excellent ones. A central finding was what he called Level 5 leadership. The CEOs behind these turnarounds were not the larger-than-life figures that business magazines celebrated. Collins’s own summary of the concept says “The good-to-great leaders never wanted to become larger-than-life heroes” (jimcollins.com ↗).

In the interview he argues the link is cause and effect, not chance. A celebrity CEO turns the company into “the one genius with 1,000 helpers,” and great results need leaders whose ambition is for the company rather than for themselves.
